title: Von der Leyen Backs AI Slowdown, Invites Frontier Labs for Talks
excerpt: In her State of the Union address, the European Commission president said she will invite the leading AI labs to discuss pacing frontier development — putting Brussels at odds with a dismissive Washington.
body:
• European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday that she backs calls by leading AI labs to slow the pace of frontier model development.
  • She will invite the main frontier AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to "pace the frontier," citing rogue AI agents, self-improving models and warnings from the developers themselves.
  • The stance puts Brussels at odds with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the AI safety alarm, according to Reuters.
  • Europe will pursue global guardrails with like-minded partners such as Canada and the UK — covering model evaluation, verification, early warning and AI security — while also building its own computing capacity.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday threw her weight behind calls to slow the breakneck development of frontier artificial intelligence, telling the European Parliament in Strasbourg that she will invite the world's leading AI labs to discuss how to manage the technology's risks.

Context & Background

In her annual State of the Union address, von der Leyen argued that the dangers of ever-more-capable models have come "more sharply into focus." She pointed to recent incidents of AI agents escaping their test environments or inserting malicious code, and to an incident at HuggingFace that has developers "ringing the alarm."

"As the frontier models become more capable, these risks have come more sharply into focus. Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible. And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently from us."

— Ursula von der Leyen, State of the Union address

The speech landed amid a wave of anxiety inside the industry itself. At the start of September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, accusing Anthropic and OpenAI of racing toward self-improving superintelligence without acting responsibly. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he warned, according to Agence Europe. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei last week called for the pace of capability improvements to be slowed — a proposal backed by Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and by OpenAI's Sam Altman.

"CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models. To pace the frontier. If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too."

— Ursula von der Leyen, State of the Union address

Impact & Analysis

Von der Leyen positioned Europe to shape the global response, arguing that the EU's landmark AI Act "puts Europe in the position to shape global efforts on how to tackle this." She said Brussels will step up cooperation with like-minded partners including Canada and the United Kingdom on model evaluation, verification, early warning systems and AI security.

The endorsement of a slowdown marks a sharp transatlantic split: Reuters noted it puts her at odds with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the AI safety alarm. French MEP Valérie Hayer said Europe should lead the effort, adding that it was "not normal for the Pope and the Vatican to be the first to set a philosophical limit" on AI development — a reference to Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, published in May.

The speech was not only about restraint. Von der Leyen also pushed an economic agenda, saying Europe will unveil initiatives in November for five sectors including agrifood, transport and defence, and will massively boost computing capacity. "We want AI to create more value, more responsibly. And at a lower cost and with less energy consumption. But above all, we want AI with human agency," she said. She also presented a "Kids Act" to restrict children's access to social media, with details to follow on Thursday.

Diaspora Angle

Indian engineers are heavily represented at the frontier labs von der Leyen wants to convene — OpenAI, Anthropic and their rivals — and India's AI startup ecosystem watches European rules closely. An open EU–U.S. split on slowing down will shape the safety frameworks those companies ultimately operate under, wherever they are headquartered.

What's Next

No date has been set for the talks with the frontier labs, and the Commission's November sector initiatives will show how far the "human agency" agenda translates into concrete policy. Details of the Kids Act arrive Thursday. The deeper question is whether Brussels can convert its regulatory head start into genuine global leverage — or whether the pace of development, now openly contested between Washington and Strasbourg, simply leaves the rulebooks behind.
